t: Corporate milestones and achievements, 2008 to 2024
b:

Fiber@Home's journey reflects a consistent record of firsts in Bangladesh's ICT and telecommunications sector:
2008 — Country's first and largest private NTTN (Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network).
2012 — Licensed as a separate vertical under Fiber@Home Global Limited (FGL).

In recognition of leadership in the sector, the Chairman, Moynul Haque Siddiqui, was honored with the ICT Businessperson of the Year award by The Daily Star ICT Awards in 2022.

t: Moynul Haque Siddiqui, Chairman
b: Moynul Haque Siddiqui is Chairman of Fiber@Home Limited. Chairman of Fiber@Home; an innovative entrepreneur who has made significant contributions to the growth of the ICT sector over the past 25 years. He founded BDCOM Online, one of Bangladesh's first nationwide Internet Services Provider (ISP). He pioneered the concept of Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) and founded Fiber@Home Limited, the country's first NTTN company. In collaboration with Bangladesh Hi-Tech Park Authority, he has steered the industrialization of the ICT sector, and then initiated Felicity IDC Limited, the first private sector Tier III Certified Data Centre. In recognition of his exceptional contributions, he was honored with the esteemed award for ICT Businessperson of the Year by The Daily Star ICT Awards in 2022.

t: Brig Gen Md. Rafiqur Rahman, psc (retd), Managing Director
b: Brig Gen Md. Rafiqur Rahman, psc (retd) is Managing Director of Fiber@Home Limited. Managing Director at Fiber@Home. He has been with the company since inception and is a pillar of strength from his vast experience and knowledge of communications infrastructure and topologies. He was previously Head of Operations and has a deep understanding of field activities. Prior to Fiber@Home, he was commander of various units at Bangladesh Army, and was also Director of Operations & Training at Border Guard; DG of Bangladesh National Cadet Corps; DG of Fire Service & Civil Defense; and Chief Instructor of School of Signal, which is responsible for communications of Bangladesh Army. He is a graduate of Defense Command and Staff College.

t: Azad Chowdhury, Additional Managing Director & CEO
b: Azad Chowdhury is Additional Managing Director & CEO of Fiber@Home Limited. Additional Managing Director (AMD) & Chief Executive Officer (CEO) at Fiber@Home. Prior to joining Fiber@Home, he had experience in development finance, global investment banking, private equity and financial inclusion technologies. His international career spans leadership roles at global investment banks across New York, Toronto, Hong Kong and Singapore spanning 20+ years, and he has nearly a decade of experience managing technology companies in Bangladesh through private equity funds. He is an alumnus of Harvard Business School (USA). At Fiber@Home Group, he is driving synergistic activities across the portfolio of businesses and building the next generation of platform services to accelerate digital lifestyle for citizens in Bangladesh, including infrastructure projects for Smart City and Smart Government.

t: Sumon Ahmed Sabir, Deputy Managing Director & CIO
b: Sumon Ahmed Sabir is Deputy Managing Director & CIO of Fiber@Home Limited. Deputy Managing Director (DMD) & Chief Information Officer (CIO) of Fiber@Home Ltd. and has been at the center of Bangladesh's Internet community for 29 years, leading the establishment of Bangladesh's IXP, CERT, and NOG. He served as MAG Member of the UN Internet Governance Forum, and as the Policy Chair for APNIC. Presently he is serving as an Executive Council Member of the Asia Pacific Network Operation Center (APNIC).

t: Sharful Alam, Deputy Managing Director & CSO
b: Sharful Alam is Deputy Managing Director & CSO of Fiber@Home Limited. Deputy Managing Director (DMD) & Chief Strategy Officer (CSO) at Fiber@Home. Since joining Fiber@Home in 2021, he has been instrumental in shaping the company's strategic direction. With over 27 years of industry experience, primarily at Aamra Networks Limited, Sharful brings a wealth of knowledge and expertise to his role. He climbed the corporate ladder at Aamra Networks Limited, ultimately assuming the role of Chief Operating Officer (COO) for over 10 years, and his strategic vision was further refined during his tenure as Director and Chief Strategy Officer at Dotlines. An IBA graduate, his academic foundation combined with his extensive industry experience positions him as a valuable asset to Fiber@Home, and his strategic guidance is instrumental in shaping the company's future growth and market leadership.

t: Akter Ul Alam, Chief Implementation & Operations Officer
b: Akter Ul Alam is Chief Implementation & Operations Officer of Fiber@Home Limited. Akter Ul Alam has over 25 years of experience in wireless, optical transmission, DWDM, and IP technologies. He has played a key role in developing Bangladesh's broadband backbone and access infrastructure. As the founder of WEEE Society Bangladesh, he advocates for formal e-waste management. Currently, he is the Chief Implementation & Operations Officer (CIOO) at Fiber@Home Ltd., overseeing the primary transmission services for various providers and also playing a role as CTO. He previously served as CSO at Fiber@Home and was Head of Transmission Planning at Grameenphone. He holds degrees from BUET and Concordia University.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 1. Telecom Sector Overview in Bangladesh
b: Bangladesh's telecommunications sector is one of the fastest-growing segments of the national economy, underpinned by a population of over 160 million and rising smartphone and internet penetration. The sector has evolved from a state-monopoly system under the former Bangladesh Telegraph & Telephone Board (now BTCL) into a liberalized, multi-operator market spanning mobile telephony, fixed broadband, nationwide transmission infrastructure, and value-added digital services. Mobile services still account for the bulk of overall connectivity, while data and internet services now represent the largest and fastest-growing share of sector revenue, reflecting a structural shift from voice to data-driven demand. Government initiatives under the "Digital Bangladesh" agenda, including planned 5G deployment led by state-owned Teletalk, are expected to further accelerate this shift.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 2. Key Market Players & Operators
b:
Mobile Network Operators (MNOs): Grameenphone, Robi Axiata, Banglalink, and the state-owned Teletalk.
Fixed-line / PSTN: Bangladesh Telecommunications Company Limited (BTCL) — state-owned, the largest fixed-line operator and former monopoly incumbent.
NTTN Operators: Fiber@Home, Summit Communications, and BTCL are the principal licensed nationwide transmission backbone providers.
Internet Service Providers (ISPs): over 900 licensed operators represented by ISPAB, ranging from national ISPs to local/regional broadband providers.
Mobile Financial Services (MFS) providers: bKash (market leader), Nagad, Rocket, and others, increasingly integrated with telecom operators' distribution networks.
Gateway/Interconnection licensees: operators holding IIG, IGW, and (historically) ICX licenses that carry international and inter-operator traffic.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 3. Industry Value Chain (NTTN, ISP, IIG, ICX, etc.)
b:
Bangladesh's telecom value chain runs from international bandwidth acquisition through nationwide transport to last-mile delivery:
IIG (International Internet Gateway): brings international internet bandwidth into Bangladesh via submarine cable landing stations and terrestrial links, and sells it downstream to ISPs and other licensees.
NTTN (Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network): the fibre-optic backbone that transports bandwidth nationwide under open-access obligations — Fiber@Home's core license (see Chapter 4).
ICX (Interconnection Exchange) / IGW (International Gateway): route and interconnect voice and data traffic between operators, and manage international voice call origination/termination.
ISPs and MNOs: deliver last-mile internet and mobile connectivity respectively to residential, enterprise, and institutional end users.
Fiber@Home operates at the NTTN and IIG layers of this chain, supplying wholesale transmission and international bandwidth capacity to downstream ISPs, MNOs, and enterprises rather than serving retail end users directly.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 4. Market Size & Growth Trends
b:
Bangladesh's telecommunications services market was valued at approximately USD 4.9 billion in 2025, with industry forecasts projecting continued growth at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of roughly 4.3% through the early 2030s.
Data and internet services account for the largest and fastest-growing share of sector revenue — around 44% of total 2025 revenue — reflecting the ongoing shift from voice to data consumption.
Mobile internet subscribers number well over 120 million, with 4G connections making up roughly half of all mobile subscriptions and continuing to grow as 3G/2G usage declines.
Rising smartphone penetration, expanding 4G coverage, early-stage 5G rollout (led by Teletalk), and growth in mobile financial services, e-commerce, and enterprise digitalization are the principal demand drivers for the sector.
Rising spectrum costs, periodic network restriction directives, and tightening regulatory/compliance requirements are recurring headwinds cited by operators and industry analysts.
This growth trajectory directly benefits infrastructure-layer licensees such as Fiber@Home, since rising data consumption and network expansion increase demand for nationwide transmission (NTTN) and international bandwidth (IIG) capacity.

ISPAB (Internet Service Providers Association of Bangladesh): represents over 900 member ISPs; advocates on broadband policy, bandwidth pricing, and licensing issues affecting internet service providers.
BASIS (Bangladesh Association of Software and Information Services): trade body for the software and IT/ITES industry, which increasingly intersects with telecom infrastructure and connectivity providers.
BCS (Bangladesh Computer Samity): trade association for the computer hardware, networking equipment, and IT retail trade.
These associations, together with BTRC and the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology (MoPTIT), form the principal institutional stakeholders that Fiber@Home engages with on industry policy matters.

t: 6. BTRC Mandate & Structure
b: The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) is the independent regulator established under the Bangladesh Telecommunication Act, 2001 to license, regulate, and oversee all telecommunication systems and services in the country — including spectrum allocation, tariff approval, quality-of-service enforcement, and dispute resolution. It is governed by a five-member commission (a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson, and additional commissioners) drawn from legal, technical, and administrative backgrounds. A full account of BTRC's establishment, leadership, statutory powers, and organizational structure is provided in Chapter 1 ("Bangladesh's Telecommunications Regulatory System") and Chapter 2 ("BTRC Organizational Structure") of this guide.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 1.2 Legal Foundation
b:
The core legislation governing Bangladesh's telecommunications sector is the Bangladesh Telecommunication Act, 2001. The legislative purpose of this Act is:
"An Act to provide for the establishment of an independent Commission for the purpose of development and efficient regulation of telecommunication system and telecommunication services in Bangladesh and matters ancillary thereto."
Through the establishment of an independent regulatory commission, this Act transferred regulatory authority from the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MoPT) to the BTRC, aiming to ensure an efficient and well-regulated telecommunications system through open competition among private operators and appropriate industry oversight.

b: BTRC operates through multiple directorates and divisions, each responsible for specific regulatory functions. The commission has been working to expand its regulatory services across the country by setting up offices at all eight divisional headquarters.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.2 What is NTTN?
b:
According to BTRC guidelines, NTTN refers to a national fibre backbone and duct infrastructure with open access obligations, rights-of-way across highways, railways, and utilities, with strict QoS and sharing rules.
The objectives of the NTTN include:
De-cluttering city areas and towns from hazardous overhead optical fibres
Minimizing the waste of national resources from developing individual networks
Providing network infrastructure on a rental basis to licensed operators

s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.4.2 Prohibition on Direct Service to Users
b:
NTTN licensees will not be allowed to provide telecommunication services directly to users. Access Network Service (ANS) operators and licensed telecom operators can use the NTTN resources to provide telecommunication services for users.
ANS operators include PSTN, cellular, cable service providers, broadband service providers, ISPs and others who provide telecom services directly to users.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.4.3 Rollout Obligations
b:
NTTN licensees have a rollout obligation to take the network up to upazila headquarters.
Year | Rollout Target
Within 3 years | All district headquarters
Within 5 years | All upazila headquarters
By 10th year | 100% of all upazilas
If the rollout obligation targets are not met, the Commission shall call on the Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) for the amount indicated.
Fiber@Home deposited Tk 10 crore as PBG (Performance Bank Guarantee) in accordance with these obligations.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.4.4 Foreign Shareholding Limit
b:
Originally, foreign shareholding was limited to a maximum of 60%.
However, BTRC has revised the NTTN guidelines, raising the foreign shareholding limit to a maximum of 70% in any NTTN operator.
Key Foreign Investment Requirements:
Foreign shareholders must invest in foreign currency directly equal to their ownership
No loans from Bangladeshi financial institutions (banks, leasing companies) can be raised for the foreign portion of investment
For NRBs (non-resident Bangladeshis), BTRC has approved a maximum of 70% of investment
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.4.5 IPO Requirement
b:
According to NTTN licensing guidelines, an operator must file for an Initial Public Offering (IPO) within five years of obtaining the licence.
No transfer of shares is allowed before the issuance of the IPO without prior written permission from the commission.

s: Chapter 4: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network (NTTN) License
t: 4.6.1 IPO Compliance Issue
b:
Despite being mandated to float shares on the stock market several years ago, five of the six NTTN operators (including Fiber@Home) have not gone public.
In a letter sent in May, BTRC asked Fiber@Home to take steps to float shares.
Fiber@Home's Chairman Moynul Haque Siddiqui stated that the company planned to go public long ago but the previous government's decision to change the IPO valuation method discouraged companies from going public.
The company expects to issue an IPO by December.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 5.2.5 Bandwidth Import Restrictions
b:
Under the revised IIG licensing guidelines, each IIG operator must ensure that no more than 50% of their total internet traffic is routed through International Terrestrial Cables (ITCs).
This represents a reduction from the previous 60% cap.
Background: In recent years, India has installed Content Delivery Network (CDN) servers within its territory, enabling faster traffic delivery through ITC cables. While submarine cable bandwidth costs Tk 220 per Mbps, Indian bandwidth costs only Tk 100 per Mbps. Bangladesh spends nearly $40 million (approximately Tk 4.88 billion) annually on importing bandwidth from India.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 5.2.6 Reporting Obligations

IIG licensees must submit monthly reports including, but not limited to:
Five-minute average incoming and outgoing traffic for each international backbone link
Daily traffic statistics
Other reports as specified by BTRC

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 5.3 Prohibition on ISP Operations

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 6.1 Overview
b: Fiber@Home Global Ltd has also obtained an International Terrestrial Cable (ITC) license. According to BTRC guidelines, a maximum of three ITC licenses were to be issued. However, in practice, seven companies received licenses, including Fiber@Home Global Ltd.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 6.2.1 Revenue Sharing
b:
ITC licensees must now pay 3% of their annual audited gross revenue on a quarterly basis, with payments due within the first 10 days of the following quarter.
This represents an increase from the previous 1% requirement.
Key Revenue Sharing Provisions:
The total amount will be reconciled annually based on audited financial statements
If underpayment is identified, the balance must be cleared within 90 days of the financial year-end
In case of overpayment, licensees can adjust the excess amount against future quarterly payments
BTRC retains the authority to revise the revenue-sharing percentage at any time
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 6.2.2 License Fees

src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 6.3 ITC Market Context
b:
ITC operators bring bandwidth via fibre optic cables from India. Currently, seven ITC operators supply most of the country's 6,500 Gbps bandwidth demand from India.
BTRC Chairman Md Emdad ul Bari stated that the revenue-sharing rate was increased to bring balance to the market as submarine cable companies are required to provide 3% in revenue sharing. He added that ITC operators have been enjoying undue benefits.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 7.1 NTTN and IIG Operators Cannot Operate as ISPs
b:
According to BTRC rules, NTTN and IIG operators cannot run business as Internet Service Providers (ISPs) .
Critical Compliance Point: NTTN and IIG operators are strictly prohibited from providing internet services directly to end users. This is a fundamental restriction of their licenses.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 7.2 NTTN Licensees Cannot Provide Direct Service to Users

src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 7.3 Infrastructure Sharing Restrictions
b:
According to clause 4.7 of the infrastructure sharing guidelines, operators (except NTTN licensees) will not be permitted to build/wired backbone transmission network, if such networks of NTTN operators were already available.
However, clause 4.8(a) of the infrastructure sharing guidelines states that telecom operators may jointly or individually develop, maintain and operate optical/wired backbone transmission network with the approval of the commission if NTTN operators fail to provide them with transmission network facility.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 7.4 Consequences of Violation
b:
Providing ISP services without the required license constitutes a serious violation. BTRC has the authority to:
Impose financial penalties
Initiate legal action under the Telecom Act
Cancel the company's NTTN license

BTRC ordered International Internet Gateway (IIG) service providers to disconnect bandwidth connections of 286 internet service providers for not converting their licences in accordance with guidelines.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 9.2 BTRC's Infrastructure Sharing Enforcement

BTRC turned down proposals of mobile phone operators Grameenphone and Banglalink to reinstall fibre optic cable for highway development activities.
The commission decided to ask NTTN operators to settle any proposals for installation or reinstallation of fibre optic cable of the mobile phone operators within 30 days.
This decision was based on the NTTN licensing guidelines and infrastructure sharing guidelines which do not allow any entity except NTTN operators to install or reinstall fibre optic cable.

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 11.2 Quality of Service (QoS) Standards
b:
Under BTRC regulations, service providers must comply with specified Quality of Service (QoS) benchmarks. The QoS Regulations, 2024, establish comprehensive standards.
Key QoS Requirements:
Service providers shall meet the QoS standards outlined in the regulations
BTRC conducts monthly network performance and health monitoring
Operators must submit monthly reports on three key indicators: accessibility, retainability, and network integrity
4G Service QoS Standards:
Minimum 4G download speed: 10 Mbps
4G upload speed: At least 2 Mbps
4G data connection success rate: 98.5% at district level
Call Quality Standards:
Call setup success rates (nationwide): 99%
Call setup success rates (district/upazila): 98%
Call drop rates (2G, national): Not exceeding 1%
Call drop rates (2G, upazila): Not exceeding 1.5%
Customer Service Standards:
Customer service calls must be answered within 90 seconds
At least 90% of calls to service centres must be answered within 40 seconds
Customer complaint resolution (non-network issues): Within 28 days
90% of customer complaints must be resolved within 5 working days
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 15.1 Legal Basis
b:
Section 63(1) and (3) of the Act clearly give BTRC the right to impose an administrative fine.
Section 64 allows the commission to impose up to Tk 100 crore for violation of its direction.
Section 65 allows BTRC to impose administrative fines up to Tk 300 crore for violation of the telecom act.
src: BTRC License Rules & Compliance Guide (Knowledge Vault – Mehedi Bhai)

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: 15.2 Procedural Steps
b:
Investigation: BTRC's Enforcement and Inspection Directorate conducts inspections and collects evidence
Show Cause Notice: The suspected violator is issued a show cause notice
Response: The alleged violator has an opportunity to respond to the notice
Determination: BTRC determines the fine based on the nature and extent of the violation
Fine Notice: BTRC issues a notice under section 65(2) stating the amount of the fine
Payment Deadline: The violator is asked to pay the fine within a prescribed time limit
Appeal: Licensees may appeal the decision

c: Regulatory Framework & Bangladesh Telecom Industry Overview
t: Phase 1: The 2025 Draft Proposal - Three Core Categories
b:
In April 2025, BTRC published a draft policy proposing to consolidate over 20 existing license types into three main categories to simplify regulations and reduce costs. The three proposed categories were:
National Infrastructure and Connectivity Service Provider (NICSP): Focused on building and leasing nationwide telecom infrastructure, such as optical fiber networks, towers, and transmission facilities, to Access Network Service Providers (ANSPs). This aimed to reduce redundant investments and lower operational costs. Under this initial draft, foreign ownership for NICSPs was proposed at up to 70%.
International Connectivity Service Provider (ICSP): Unified all international connectivity services, replacing legacy permits like submarine cable and International Gateway (IGW) licenses.
Access Network Service Provider (ANSP): Consolidated mobile and fixed-line services for direct end-user connectivity.

ICSP Split into Two: The ICSP license was divided into two new categories:
Facility-based ICSP
Non-facility-based ICSP (with lower fees)
FTSP Restructured: The Fixed Telecom Service Provider (FTSP) license was also restructured into two separate categories for Internet Service Providers at the nationwide and district levels.

t: What does DWDM stand for, and what is its basic principle?
b: Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing. Many optical signals, each on its own wavelength (colour) of light, are combined onto one fibre pair and separated again at the far end.

t: Which wavelength band does DWDM mainly use, and why?
b: The C-band, roughly 1530 to 1565 nm. Fibre loss is lowest there, and erbium-doped fibre amplifiers work in that band.

t: What channel spacing does DWDM use?
b: A tight ITU-T grid (G.694.1), typically 100 GHz or 50 GHz, which is about 0.8 nm or 0.4 nm. This gives 40 to 96 or more channels in the C-band.

t: How does DWDM differ from CWDM?
b: CWDM uses 20 nm spacing with up to 18 channels, needs no cooled lasers, costs less and suits short unamplified links. DWDM packs far more channels and can be amplified for long distances.

t: Name the main building blocks of a DWDM system.
b: Transponders or muxponders, multiplexer and demultiplexer, optical amplifiers, dispersion compensation where needed, and OADM or ROADM nodes that add and drop wavelengths.

t: What is the difference between a transponder and a muxponder?
b: A transponder converts one client signal into one DWDM wavelength. A muxponder combines several lower-rate client signals, such as ten 10G, into one higher-rate wavelength such as 100G.

t: What does an EDFA do, and why is it important?
b: An Erbium-Doped Fibre Amplifier boosts all C-band wavelengths together in the optical domain, with no conversion to electrical. It lets a link span hundreds of kilometres, with amplifier sites roughly every 80 to 100 km.

t: What is a ROADM and why does it matter?
b: A Reconfigurable Optical Add-Drop Multiplexer. The operator can add, drop or pass through any wavelength at a site remotely, by software, without manual re-patching.

t: What is OTN, and how does it relate to DWDM?
b: Optical Transport Network (ITU-T G.709). It is the digital wrapper carried on each wavelength, adding framing, forward error correction, performance monitoring and sub-wavelength switching (ODU containers).

t: What is Forward Error Correction (FEC)?
b: Extra coding bits sent with the data so the receiver can correct bit errors itself. A wavelength can then travel further, or run at a higher rate, for the same optical signal quality.

t: Which impairments limit a DWDM link?
b: Attenuation, chromatic dispersion, polarisation mode dispersion, accumulated amplifier noise (falling OSNR), and non-linear effects such as four-wave mixing when channel power is high.

t: What is coherent transmission?
b: A technique that encodes data on the phase and polarisation of light and uses digital signal processing at the receiver. It enables 100G, 200G and 400G per wavelength and compensates dispersion electronically.

t: What is the Optical Supervisory Channel (OSC)?
b: A separate wavelength outside the amplifier band, commonly 1510 nm, that carries management and monitoring information between sites. It stays up even when no traffic channels are lit.

t: Give typical use cases of DWDM for a transmission operator.
b: Long-haul and inter-city backbone, metro core rings, submarine cable backhaul, data-centre interconnect, leasing whole wavelengths to operators, and relieving fibre exhaust by multiplying capacity on existing fibre.

t: What does SDH stand for, and what is its North American equivalent?
b: Synchronous Digital Hierarchy. The North American equivalent is SONET. Both are time-division multiplexing (TDM) transport systems locked to a common clock.

t: What technology did SDH replace, and what was the main improvement?
b: PDH (Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy). SDH is synchronous, so a single E1 can be added or dropped directly from a high-rate stream without demultiplexing every level, and it added standard management overhead.

t: What are the SDH rate levels?
b: STM-1 is 155.52 Mbps, STM-4 is 622 Mbps, STM-16 is about 2.5 Gbps and STM-64 is about 10 Gbps. Each level is four times the previous one.

t: What is the structure of an STM-1 frame?
b: 9 rows by 270 columns of bytes, sent 8,000 times per second (every 125 microseconds). The first 9 columns hold section overhead and pointers; the rest is payload.

t: How is an E1 carried inside SDH?
b: A 2.048 Mbps E1 is mapped into a container (C-12), given path overhead to become a virtual container (VC-12), aligned into tributary units, and multiplexed into a VC-4 and the STM-1 frame. One STM-1 carries 63 E1s.

t: What are the layers of SDH overhead?
b: Regenerator section overhead (RSOH), multiplex section overhead (MSOH) and path overhead (POH). They carry framing, error monitoring, protection signalling and management channels.

t: What are the main SDH network elements?
b: Terminal multiplexer, add-drop multiplexer (ADM), digital cross-connect (DXC) and regenerator.

t: How does SDH protect traffic, and how fast?
b: Through ring and linear protection such as SNCP, MS-SPRing and 1+1 MSP, with switchover within 50 ms. This figure became the benchmark for later technologies.

t: Why does SDH need synchronisation, and how is it distributed?
b: All nodes must run from the same clock or data slips occur. A primary reference clock feeds the network, and each node recovers timing from the line or from a synchronisation supply unit.

t: How was SDH adapted to carry Ethernet?
b: With Ethernet over SDH: GFP encapsulates the frames, virtual concatenation (VCAT) bundles containers into the needed bandwidth, and LCAS resizes that bundle without interrupting traffic.

t: Why is SDH called legacy?
b: It is built for fixed-rate TDM circuits, so it carries bursty packet traffic inefficiently, it tops out near 10G, and much of the equipment is reaching end of vendor support.

t: Where is SDH still relevant?
b: Existing E1 and STM leased lines, older 2G and 3G backhaul, utility and railway networks, and as a clock reference. The MPLS deck lists SDH, SONET and E1 among the services MPLS was designed to carry.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What does MPLS stand for, and in which decade did it appear?
b: Multi Protocol Label Switching. It was born in IPv4 networking in the 1990s.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What were the main challenges of data networks before MPLS?
b: Heterogeneous vendor models with proprietary protocols, and many separate types of communication: layer 2 (MAC based), layer 3 (IP based), SDH, SONET and E1.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: Why is MPLS called an "umbrella protocol"?
b: It carries all kinds of layer 2, layer 3, SDH, SONET and E1 communication over one common network architecture.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What customer-separation benefit does MPLS give a service provider?
b: Different customers can use duplicate MAC addresses, IP addresses and VLANs without disturbing each other's communication.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What did MPLS add in the 2010s?
b: MPLS in IPv6 networking. It solved the IPv4 capacity limitation and allowed Dual-Stack (IPv4 and IPv6) on the same network architecture.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: How is an IPv4 address structured?
b: It is a 32-bit number written as 4 octets, for example 192.168.10.1.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What does a subnet mask of /30 mean, and how is it written in dotted decimal?
b: 30 bits of the address are fixed and 2 bits can vary. In dotted decimal it is 255.255.255.252.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: In network 192.168.10.0/30, name the network IP, the host IPs and the broadcast IP.
b: Network IP 192.168.10.0, host IPs 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.10.2, broadcast IP 192.168.10.3. Only 2 of the 4 addresses are usable.

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: What are the usable IPs of the next /30 network, 192.168.10.4/30?

s: IP/MPLS 3.1 IP basics and why MPLS exists
t: How do L2 and L3 communication differ?
b: L2 is MAC-based and works inside the same broadcast domain and VLAN. In L3, IPs of the same network talk without routing, and IPs of different networks talk through routing.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: What three types of network topology does the deck describe?
b: Pure switch-based network, pure router-based network, and mixed network.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: What do CE, PE and P stand for?
b: CE is Client Edge, PE is Provider Edge, and P is Provider (a core router with no customer connection).

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: Where is the IP peering in an L2 service?
b: Between CE and CE. The provider only carries the frames, so the two customer devices peer directly.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: Where is the IP peering in an L3 service?
b: Between PE and CE. The provider edge router takes part in the customer's routing.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: What kind of duplication appears in L2 and in L3 services?
b: L2 services face duplicate VLANs. L3 services face duplicate IPs.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: In the Dhaka core and district access ring example, which address range is duplicated between clients?
b: 192.168.100.0/24 (192.168.100.1 and 192.168.100.2) is used by more than one client between their AGG and Branch sites.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: Why is a duplicate customer IP a problem on a plain routed backbone?
b: A single routing table can hold only one path for a prefix, so two clients using 192.168.100.0/24 would collide and their traffic could not be told apart.

s: IP/MPLS 3.2 Topologies, roles and the duplication problem
t: What solution do both decks give for carrying L2 and L3 customers with duplicate addressing on one backbone?
b: MPLS, using VRFs for L3 customers and L2 tunnels (Xconnect/pseudowire, VPLS) for L2 customers.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: Which subnet masks are used for loopback IPs and for point-to-point links in the backbone?
b: Loopbacks use /32 (for example 10.255.10.2/32). Point-to-point links use /30 (for example 10.11.10.1/30 and 10.11.10.2/30).

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: Which routing protocol builds reachability inside the backbone, and what does its name mean?
b: OSPF, Open Shortest Path First. It advertises the loopbacks and link networks between the backbone routers.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: What metric does OSPF use to choose a path?
b: Cost. Each link has a cost (the deck shows values such as 1, 5, 30 and 60) and OSPF picks the path with the lowest total cost.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: In the lab, what OSPF costs are set on the Badda-PE to Badda-P link, the Badda-P to MGRE-P link, and the GRE tunnel?
b: Cost 1 on Badda-PE to Badda-P, cost 10 on Badda-P to MGRE-P, and cost 500 on the tunnel.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: What are the loopback addresses of the four lab routers in the L3VPN example?

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: Which three networks connect those four routers?
b: 10.51.1.16/30 between Badda-PE and Badda-P, 10.50.1.24/30 between Badda-P and MGRE-P, and 10.33.16.0/21 on the multipoint GRE tunnel between MGRE-P and NTTN-PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: Which OSPF areas are used in the lab?
b: The backbone links and loopbacks are in area 0.0.0.0. The tunnel network 10.33.16.0/21 and the NTTN-PE loopback are in area 0.0.0.2.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: What does BGP stand for, and what is its job in the MPLS VPN design?
b: Border Gateway Protocol. It runs between PE loopbacks and carries customer routes as VPNv4 routes (MP-BGP).

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: What is a Route Reflector (RR) and which router plays that role in the lab?
b: An RR receives VPNv4 routes from one PE and reflects them to the others, so PEs peer only with the RR instead of with every other PE. Badda-P (10.35.1.1) is the RR, with Badda-PE and NTTN-PE configured as reflect-clients.

s: IP/MPLS 3.3 Backbone routing: OSPF, loopbacks, BGP and the route reflector
t: Which BGP AS number is used in the lab, and why does the PE configuration include update-source Loopback0?
b: AS 65000 on all routers (iBGP). update-source Loopback0 makes the session use the loopback address, which stays reachable through OSPF whichever physical link is up.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What does VRF stand for and what does it do?
b: Virtual Routing and Forwarding. It is a separate routing table inside a PE router, one per customer, so customers with the same prefixes stay isolated.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What three parameters define a VRF in the decks?
b: A name, a Route Distinguisher (RD), and Route Targets (import and export).

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What is the role of the Route Distinguisher?
b: The RD creates a separate VRF routing table inside the router and is prepended to the customer prefix, making it unique in the backbone even when another customer uses the same IPv4 network.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: How many bits are an IPv4 route, an RD and a VPNv4 route?
b: IPv4 route 32 bits, RD 64 bits, VPNv4 route 96 bits (RD plus IPv4).

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: With RD 58587:10 and IPv4 network 192.168.100.0/24, what is the VPNv4 network?

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What is a route target?
b: A BGP extended community that decides whether a VPNv4 route is accepted into a specific VRF.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What must match for a PE to accept a VPNv4 route from a remote PE?
b: The route-target export of the sending PE must match the route-target import of the receiving PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: In deck 1, how are the route targets of VRF A set on the two PEs?
b: One PE imports 58587:10 and exports 58587:100. The other imports 58587:100 and exports 58587:10, so each side's export equals the other side's import. Both use RD 58587:10.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: How does VRF B differ from VRF A in deck 1?
b: VRF B uses RD 58587:20 with route targets 58587:20 and 58587:200, so its routes never enter VRF A even when the customer prefixes are identical.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: What are the VRF name, RD and route targets in the lab (deck 2)?
b: VRF FSIBL with rd 65000:69, route-target export 65000:69 and route-target import 65000:69 on both Badda-PE and NTTN-PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: In the lab, what is the customer route in its IPv4 and VPNv4 forms?
b: 10.69.1.52/30 is the 32-bit IPv4 route in the FSIBL VRF table. 65000:69:10.69.1.52/30 is the 96-bit VPNv4 route carried by MP-BGP.

s: IP/MPLS 3.4 VRF, route distinguisher, route target and VPNv4
t: How do customer routes get from the VRF into BGP, and why does the PE need send-community extended?
b: The VRF's IPv4 routes are redistributed into BGP (redistribute connected and redistribute static under address-family ipv4 vrf FSIBL). send-community extended is needed because route targets are extended communities; without it the remote PE could not match its import.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: What two planes make up a router's data handling structure?
b: The control plane and the data plane (also called the forwarding plane).

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: Which protocols run in the control plane of an MPLS L3VPN router?
b: Routing protocols (OSPF and BGP) and the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: Which tables belong to the data plane?
b: The IP routing table, the VRF table and the MPLS forwarding table.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: What do RIB and LIB stand for?
b: Routing Information Base and Label Information Base.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: Which control-plane table does each protocol fill?
b: OSPF fills the RIB. LDP fills the LIB. BGP fills both a RIB and a LIB, because it carries the customer route and the VRF label together.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: What do FIB and LFIB stand for, and which data-plane table is each?
b: Forwarding Information Base, which is the IP routing table, and Label Forwarding Information Base, which is the MPLS forwarding table.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: Which tables does the VRF table use in the data plane?
b: Both: the FIB for the customer route and the LFIB for the labels.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: What are the two labels on an L3VPN packet, and what does each represent?
b: The inner label is the VRF (VPN) label and identifies the customer route. The outer label is the MPLS (LDP) label and follows the backbone route to the remote PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: Which protocol assigns the outer label and which assigns the inner label in L3VPN?
b: LDP assigns the outer MPLS label for backbone routes. MP-BGP assigns the inner VRF label along with the VPNv4 route.

s: IP/MPLS 3.5 Control plane and data plane tables
t: How do the decks define the local (in) label and the remote (outgoing) label?
b: The remote or outgoing label points towards the destination prefix. The local or in label is on the opposite side, facing away from the destination. Labels are counted in the direction the data packet travels.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What does LDP stand for and what does it do?
b: Label Distribution Protocol. Each router assigns a local label to backbone prefixes (the /32 loopbacks) and advertises it to its neighbours.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What is an LSP?
b: A Label Switched Path: the chain of labels, hop by hop, that a packet follows from the ingress PE to the egress PE's loopback.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: In deck 1, which LDP labels are shown for loopback 10.255.10.2/32?
b: The owner of the loopback advertises null. Moving away from it, routers hold local labels 40, 50 and 60, and each learns its neighbour's label as its remote label (for example L: 50, R: 40).

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: Why does the router that owns the destination loopback have a null label?
b: The destination IP is inside that router, so no remote label is needed and its local label is implicit null. The previous router therefore pops the outer label before delivering the packet. This behaviour is called penultimate hop popping (PHP).

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What are the three MPLS label operations?
b: Push (add a label), Swap (replace the incoming label with the outgoing one) and Pop (remove the label).

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: In the lab L3VPN, what does Badda-PE do for destination 10.45.225.109/32?
b: It has no in label and pushes outgoing label 1072.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What does Badda-P do with label 1072?
b: It swaps incoming label 1072 for outgoing label 468.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What does MGRE-P do with label 468?
b: It pops the label (the outgoing label shows as "POP Label") and sends the packet on to NTTN-PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: Which commands enable MPLS and LDP on the Badda-PE backbone interface?
b: mpls label protocol ldp and mpls ldp router-id Loopback0 force globally, then mpls ip and mpls mtu 9000 under interface BDI1254.

s: IP/MPLS 3.6 LDP labels, LSP and push, swap, pop
t: What is the purpose of mpls ldp sync under OSPF?
b: It keeps OSPF and LDP synchronised, so OSPF does not send traffic over a link until LDP labels are ready on it. This avoids dropping labelled traffic on a link that has routing but no labels.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: In deck 1, how does the label stack change as a packet for 192.168.100.2 crosses the backbone?
b: The ingress PE pushes VPN label 19 and LDP label 50 (Data | 19 | 50). The next router swaps 50 for 40 (Data | 19 | 40). The router before the egress PE pops the LDP label (Data | 19). The egress PE removes label 19 and delivers plain data.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: Which label stays unchanged from ingress PE to egress PE, and why?
b: The inner VPN label (19 in deck 1, 17 in the lab). P routers only look at the outer label, so the inner label reaches the egress PE and tells it which VRF the packet belongs to.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: In the lab, which VPN label does NTTN-PE assign to 10.69.1.52/30, and how does it appear on each PE?
b: Label 17. NTTN-PE holds it as In Label 17 (Out Label 0). Badda-PE learns it through the RR as Out Label 17.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: What gateway does each PE show for 10.69.1.52/30 in VRF FSIBL?
b: NTTN-PE shows Gateway = vlan69, the interface to the CE. Badda-PE shows Gateway = 10.45.225.109, the loopback of NTTN-PE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: Describe the full label stack for a packet from Badda-PE to 10.69.1.54.
b: Badda-PE sends Data | 17 | 1072. Badda-P swaps to Data | 17 | 468. MGRE-P pops to Data | 17. NTTN-PE removes 17 and forwards the plain IP packet out vlan69 to the CE.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: Why does the Badda-P router have no VRF table, even though it is the route reflector?
b: It is a P router with no customer attached. It only reflects VPNv4 routes and switches on the outer label, so it needs no VRF. The undo policy vpn-target line lets it keep VPNv4 routes without a matching local route target.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: What does the deck note about the MikroTik NTTN-PE and the VRF label?
b: MikroTik does not show the VRF label in the routing table, but label 17 is there.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: What are the five configuration stages shown for Badda-PE, in order?
b: IP (interfaces and loopback), OSPF, MPLS and LDP, VRF, and MP-BGP.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: How is a customer-facing interface placed in the VRF on Badda-PE?
b: With vrf forwarding FSIBL under interface BDI69, which has address 10.69.0.1 255.255.255.248.

s: IP/MPLS 3.7 L3VPN packet walk and configuration
t: What MTU values are used on the backbone links and on the GRE tunnel, and why do they differ?
b: Backbone interfaces use MTU 9000 (also mpls mtu 9000). The tunnel uses IP MTU 1980, with MPLS MTU 1980 on the MikroTik side, because the GRE tunnel rides over a link with a 2028 MTU and adds its own header. Larger MTUs leave room for the two MPLS labels on customer packets.

t: What is an Xconnect or pseudowire?
b: A point-to-point L2 tunnel across the MPLS backbone that joins a customer port on one PE to a customer port on another PE, so the two CEs behave as if directly connected at layer 2.

t: What three parameters define the Xconnect in deck 1?
b: The neighbor loopback IP (10.255.10.2), the VC ID or Virtual Circuit Identifier (100), and the AC or Attachment Circuit (TE0/0/10).

t: What must match on the two PEs of a pseudowire, and what is the attachment circuit?
b: The VC ID must be the same on both ends (100 in deck 1), and each PE points to the other's loopback as neighbor. The attachment circuit is the physical PE interface connected to the CE (TE0/0/10 on one side, TE0/0/12 on the other).

t: How does the L2VPN label stack compare with the L3VPN one in deck 1?
b: It is the same two-label structure: an inner VPN label (19) and an outer LDP label (50, then 40, then popped). The payload is a customer Ethernet frame, and the egress PE forwards it to the attachment circuit instead of doing a VRF route lookup.

t: Which control-plane protocols does VPLS use, and which one replaces BGP's role from L3VPN?
b: OSPF (RIB), LDP (LIB) and Targeted LDP (LIB). Targeted LDP runs directly between the two PE loopbacks and distributes the inner VC label, which is the job MP-BGP did for the VRF label.

t: What does the VPLS data plane use in place of a VRF routing table?
b: The MPLS L2 transport layer: a VPLS bridge MAC-address table for the customer plus the LFIB. Forwarding is by customer MAC address, not IP route.

t: In the lab VPLS, what are the outer-label operations towards NTTN-PE (10.45.225.169)?
b: Badda-PE pushes 1389, Badda-P swaps 1389 for 304, and MGRE-P pops 304.

t: What are the VC ID and the inner VC labels of VPLS-Mongla, and what is the label stack from Badda-PE?
b: VC ID 210. Badda-PE has Out Label 278 and In Label 20; NTTN-PE has In Label 278 and Out Label 20. A frame from Badda-PE travels as Data | 278 | 1389, then Data | 278 | 304, then Data | 278, and NTTN-PE delivers it to bridge Loopback_VPLS.

t: What are the building blocks of the VPLS configuration on Badda-PE?
b: A pseudowire class (pw-pcl with encapsulation mpls and control-word), a VFI or Virtual Forwarding Instance (l2 vfi VPLS-Mongla manual with vpn id 3977, bridge-domain 3977, mtu 9000 and neighbor 10.45.225.169 210 pw-class pw-pcl), and the attachment circuit (GigabitEthernet0/0/15 with service instance 3977 in bridge-domain 3977).

t: How is the same VPLS built on the MikroTik NTTN-PE?
b: A VPLS interface with cisco-style-id=210, remote-peer=10.45.1.17, use-controlword=yes and MTU 9000, plus a bridge named Loopback_VPLS whose ports are the VPLS interface and ether2 (the port to the CE). The deck notes MikroTik does not show the LFIB or the customer MAC table, though both exist.

t: What is MPLS traffic engineering (MPLS-TE), and what problem does it solve?
b: It steers traffic along explicitly chosen paths instead of only the lowest-cost OSPF path. This uses spare capacity on longer routes, avoids congestion on the shortest path, and can guarantee bandwidth for selected traffic.

t: Why can plain OSPF routing leave a network unevenly loaded?
b: OSPF sends all traffic for a destination along the lowest-cost path, whatever the load. One route can congest while a parallel, slightly higher-cost route sits idle.

t: Which protocols and mechanisms does MPLS-TE use?
b: OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE floods link bandwidth and attributes. CSPF (Constrained Shortest Path First) computes a path that meets the constraints. RSVP-TE signals the tunnel and reserves labels along it.

t: What is the simplest form of traffic engineering visible in the lab?
b: Tuning OSPF costs. The lab sets cost 1, 10 and 500 on different links, with auto-cost reference-bandwidth, so the operator decides which links are preferred and which are last resort.

t: What is Fast Reroute (FRR)?
b: A pre-computed backup path that takes over locally within about 50 ms when a link or node fails, before routing reconverges. The lab's P router shows the IP version of this idea with fast-reroute lfa under OSPF.

t: What is Segment Routing, and how does it change traffic engineering?
b: The ingress router encodes the path as a list of segments (labels) in the packet, distributed by the IGP itself. The core holds no per-tunnel state and needs neither LDP nor RSVP-TE, and a controller can compute the paths (SR-TE).

t: What does GPON stand for, and which standard defines it?
b: Gigabit Passive Optical Network, defined in ITU-T G.984.

t: What are the three parts of a GPON network?
b: The OLT (Optical Line Terminal) at the operator's PoP, the ODN (Optical Distribution Network) of fibre and passive splitters, and the ONT or ONU (Optical Network Terminal or Unit) at the customer premises.

t: Why is it called passive?
b: Between the OLT and the customer there is no powered equipment. Splitters divide the light without electricity, which lowers cost and maintenance in the field.

t: What are GPON's line rates and wavelengths?
b: 2.488 Gbps downstream on 1490 nm and 1.244 Gbps upstream on 1310 nm, on a single fibre. 1550 nm can carry an RF video overlay.

t: What split ratio and reach are typical?
b: One OLT port is commonly split 1:32 or 1:64 (the standard allows up to 1:128), with a physical reach of about 20 km.

t: How does downstream transmission work?
b: The OLT broadcasts to every ONT on the port. Frames are encrypted, and each ONT keeps only those carrying its own GEM port ID.

t: How does upstream transmission avoid collisions?
b: By TDMA. The OLT grants each ONT a time slot, and ranging measures each ONT's distance so its burst arrives exactly in its slot.

t: What is Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA)?
b: The OLT adjusts upstream time slots according to each ONT's current demand and its service profile, so idle subscribers do not waste shared capacity.

t: What are GEM ports and T-CONTs?
b: A GEM port identifies an individual service flow. A T-CONT (Transmission Container) is the upstream bandwidth unit that DBA allocates; GEM ports are mapped into T-CONTs according to service class.

t: How does a splitter affect the optical power budget?
b: Each 1:2 split costs about 3.5 dB, so a 1:32 splitter (five splits) loses roughly 17.5 dB and a 1:64 (six splits) about 21 dB. With common Class B+ optics the total budget is 28 dB, which limits split ratio and distance together.

t: What do FTTH, FTTB and FTTC mean?
b: Fibre to the Home, to the Building and to the Curb or Cabinet. They describe how close the fibre comes to the user before another medium takes over.

t: How does GPON differ from EPON?
b: GPON is the ITU-T standard with 2.5G/1.25G rates and GEM encapsulation. EPON is the IEEE standard (802.3ah) with symmetric 1 Gbps and native Ethernet framing, usually cheaper but with less built-in management.

t: Why does GPON suit last-mile access?
b: One feeder fibre and one OLT port serve dozens of homes or businesses, with no powered equipment in the field, so cost per subscriber is low.

t: What comes after GPON?
b: XG-PON and XGS-PON (10 Gbps), then 25G and 50G PON. They use different wavelengths, so they can share the same ODN with existing GPON.

t: Compare DWDM, SDH, IP/MPLS and GPON on layer, multiplexing, capacity and role.
b: Technology Layer Multiplexing Typical capacity Main role DWDM Layer 0/1 Wavelength 40 to 96+ channels of 10G Long-haul and (optical) to 400G per fibre pair metro backbone SDH Layer 1 (TDM) Fixed time slots 155 Mbps to 10 Gbps Legacy circuits, E1 (STM-1 to STM-64) and STM leased lines IP/MPLS Layer 2.5/3 Statistical, label Limited by interface speed Aggregation and (packet) switched (1G to 100G+) core, L2VPN and L3VPN services GPON Layer 1/2 TDM down, TDMA 2.5G down, 1.25G up, Last-mile fibre (access) up, passive split shared per port access

t: What is the difference between circuit-switched and packet-switched transport?
b: Circuit-switched transport (SDH) reserves a fixed slot whether or not data is flowing, giving guaranteed but inflexible capacity. Packet-switched transport (IP/MPLS) shares capacity statistically, so it is efficient for bursty data but needs QoS to guarantee performance.

t: Are DWDM and IP/MPLS competitors?
b: No, they are complementary layers. DWDM supplies the raw wavelengths between sites, and IP/MPLS routers use those wavelengths as links to deliver services.

t: When would an operator sell a DWDM wavelength instead of an MPLS circuit?
b: When the customer needs a large, fixed, fully dedicated capacity such as 10G or 100G between two points. MPLS circuits fit smaller or variable bandwidths, many sites, and customers who need any-to-any VPN connectivity.

t: How do protection mechanisms compare?
b: SDH gives sub-50 ms ring protection. DWDM offers optical 1+1 protection or slower ROADM restoration. IP/MPLS uses Fast Reroute (about 50 ms) plus routing reconvergence. GPON can use Type B or Type C protection with duplicated feeder fibre or OLT ports.

t: Which technology handles duplicate customer addressing, and how?
b: IP/MPLS. VRFs with route distinguishers separate duplicate IPs for L3 customers, and pseudowires or VPLS separate duplicate VLANs for L2 customers. DWDM and SDH are transparent to addressing, since each customer gets its own wavelength or time slot.

t: How does bandwidth granularity compare?
b: SDH sells fixed steps (2 Mbps E1, 155 Mbps STM-1). DWDM sells whole wavelengths (10G, 100G). IP/MPLS can sell any rate in software, such as 37 Mbps, by policing a port. GPON sells per-subscriber profiles on a shared port.

t: Which technologies give deterministic delay, and which do not?
b: DWDM and SDH give fixed, predictable delay because capacity is dedicated. IP/MPLS delay varies with queueing, so latency-sensitive services need QoS or traffic engineering. GPON upstream delay depends on DBA scheduling.

t: How are legacy E1 or SDH circuits carried over an MPLS network?
b: By circuit emulation over a pseudowire (SAToP or CESoPSN), which packetises the TDM stream. This is how MPLS acts as the "umbrella" for SDH, SONET and E1 in the deck.

t: Which technology fits each part of the network?
b: DWDM for backbone and metro core capacity, IP/MPLS for aggregation and service delivery, GPON for the last mile, and SDH only where legacy TDM services remain.

t: What is the broad sequence of transport technology evolution?
b: PDH (E1/E3), then SDH/SONET, then DWDM under SDH, then packet transport with IP/MPLS over DWDM and OTN, and now converged packet-optical networks controlled by software.

t: What timeline do the MPLS decks give for IP and MPLS?
b: IPv4 data communication began in the 1970s. MPLS arrived in IPv4 networking in the 1990s. MPLS in IPv6 networking followed in the 2010s, solving IPv4 capacity limits and enabling Dual-Stack.

t: Why are operators migrating from SDH to packet transport?
b: Traffic is now almost entirely IP, SDH tops out near 10G, equipment is reaching end of support, and one packet network can emulate the old TDM circuits while carrying data far more efficiently.

t: How has DWDM itself evolved?
b: From 2.5G and 10G direct-detection channels to coherent 100G, 200G and 400G and beyond; from fixed OADMs to ROADMs and flexible grid; and towards pluggable coherent optics (such as 400ZR) placed directly in routers.

t: What is IP over DWDM?
b: Putting coloured coherent optics straight into router ports, so the router connects to the DWDM line system without a separate transponder shelf. It removes a layer of equipment and cost.

t: What are the next steps for MPLS?
b: Segment Routing (SR-MPLS and SRv6) replacing LDP and RSVP-TE, and EVPN replacing VPLS and LDP-signalled pseudowires, with SDN controllers for path computation.

t: What role does SDN play in the roadmap?
b: A central controller sees the whole network and programs paths and services through open interfaces. This enables automated provisioning, multi-layer optimisation of IP and optical together, and faster service delivery.

t: How is access evolving, and what does 5G demand of transport?
b: Access moves from copper and point-to-point fibre to GPON, then XGS-PON and 25G/50G PON. 5G needs dense fibre to many more cell sites, higher backhaul capacity, low latency and accurate time synchronisation.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: What does NTTN stand for?
b: Nationwide Telecommunication Transmission Network.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: What is an NTTN operator?
b: A licensee authorised to build, maintain and operate a nationwide fibre-optic transmission network and lease its capacity to other licensed operators.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: Who are an NTTN operator's customers?
b: Access Network Service operators and other licensed or authorised users: mobile operators, ISPs, IIGs, IGWs, ICXs, PSTN operators and large institutions.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: Can an NTTN operator sell directly to end users?
b: No. The licensing guidelines state that NTTN licensees will not provide telecommunication services directly to end users. They are wholesale providers.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: Why was the NTTN layer created?
b: To share common infrastructure instead of every operator digging its own fibre. The aims were to avoid duplicate investment and repeated road cutting, to extend transmission beyond the big cities, and to give all operators access to the same backbone.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: What kinds of service does an NTTN operator sell?
b: Dark fibre or fibre core lease, transmission capacity (wavelengths, STM or Ethernet circuits), MPLS L2 and L3 connectivity between a client's sites, and backhaul from client sites to its PoPs.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: What is the difference between leasing dark fibre and leasing capacity?
b: Dark fibre is unlit glass: the client attaches its own equipment and controls the capacity. Leased capacity is a managed circuit of a set bandwidth, lit and monitored by the NTTN operator.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: How does an NTTN operator fit with the MPLS decks' Client AGG and Client Branch example?
b: The NTTN backbone is the provider network of PE and P routers. Each client's aggregation site and branch connect as CEs, and the NTTN separates clients with VRFs or L2 tunnels so they can use overlapping IPs and VLANs.

s: Definition and role of NTTN operators
t: Where does NTTN sit among Bangladesh's telecom licence layers?
b: It is the domestic transmission layer. International capacity comes through submarine cable and ITC operators, IIGs and IGWs handle international internet and voice, ICXs interconnect voice, and ISPs and mobile operators serve end users. NTTN links them all inside the country.

t: Which body issues NTTN licences, and under which law?
b: The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC), under the Bangladesh Telecommunication Act, 2001, with government approval.

t: When were the NTTN licensing guidelines issued?
b: On 30 November 2008.

t: How long is an NTTN licence valid?
b: The initial term is 15 years, renewable for further 5-year periods subject to the Commission's approval.

t: What one-time and annual fees do the 2008 guidelines set?
b: Application fee Tk 50,000, licence acquisition fee Tk 3 crore, and annual licence fee Tk 25 lakh.

t: What revenue share does an NTTN licensee pay to BTRC?
b: 0% in year 1, 1% in years 2 and 3, 2% in years 4 and 5, and 3% from year 6 onwards.

t: What is the rollout obligation?
b: Coverage of Upazila headquarters must rise from 5% in the first year to 100% by the tenth year.

t: What do the guidelines say about foreign ownership?
b: Foreign shareholding is capped at 60%, or 70% for non-resident Bangladeshi entities, so local partners hold at least 40% or 30% respectively.

t: What is the public listing requirement?
b: The licensee must file for an Initial Public Offering (IPO) within five years of the licence being issued. The Daily Star has reported that NTTN operators had yet to go public (only the headline was available when this set was written).

t: How is the licensing framework changing?
b: The government's 2025 telecom network and licensing reform policy aims to cut the number of network layers from six or seven to three, and to let state-owned BTCL, Bangladesh Railway and PGCB expand their fibre freely. Under the current licensing policy NTTN falls under the National Infrastructure and Connectivity Service Provider (NICSP) category, and Bangla Phone's 2026 licence was issued under the legacy framework, with migration to follow when the licensing regime changes. Check the latest BTRC notices for the current licence categories.

t: What are the usual tiers of an NTTN network?
b: Core (national backbone between major cities), aggregation or metro (district and city rings), and access (rings and last-mile links to client sites). The MPLS deck shows this as "Core Dhaka" feeding an "Access Ring District".

t: What are the technology layers of the backbone, from bottom to top?
b: The physical fibre and ducts, the optical transmission layer (DWDM, with OTN or legacy SDH), and the packet layer (IP/MPLS routers) that delivers client services.

t: What does the IP/MPLS core of the backbone consist of?
b: P routers that switch labels, PE routers at the edge holding customer VRFs and pseudowires, and route reflectors for MP-BGP. OSPF and LDP run between them on /30 point-to-point links, with /32 loopbacks identifying each router.

t: Why is a ring topology common in transmission networks?
b: A ring gives every node two directions to reach the rest of the network, so a single fibre cut does not isolate any site, while using fewer fibre routes than a full mesh.

t: When is a mesh used instead of a ring?
b: In the core between major cities, where several independent routes exist. A mesh survives multiple failures and gives shorter paths, at the cost of more fibre and ports.

t: How can a backbone reach a remote PE when no native MPLS link exists?
b: By tunnelling. In the lab, MGRE-P and NTTN-PE are joined by a multipoint GRE tunnel (10.33.16.0/21) with OSPF and LDP running over it, so labelled traffic crosses a plain IP segment.

t: Where does international connectivity join the national backbone?
b: At submarine cable landing stations (Cox's Bazar and Kuakata) and terrestrial cross-border links, from which traffic is backhauled to Dhaka over the NTTN backbone.

t: What is the role of the Network Operations Centre (NOC)?
b: It monitors the fibre, transmission and IP layers around the clock, detects and localises faults, dispatches field teams for fibre cuts, and tracks service levels against client SLAs.

t: What are the two ways of deploying fibre, and how do they compare?
b: Underground (ducted or buried) fibre costs more and takes longer to build but is better protected. Overhead (aerial) fibre on poles is cheaper and quicker but more exposed to cuts and weather.

t: What is a Point of Presence (PoP)?
b: A physical site where the operator houses transmission and routing equipment and where clients can connect to the network.

t: What equipment is typically found in a PoP?
b: Optical distribution frames, DWDM or SDH nodes, MPLS routers or switches, OLTs for GPON, and supporting power (rectifiers, batteries, generator), cooling and security.

t: How are PoPs usually classified?
b: By hierarchy: core PoPs in major cities, aggregation PoPs at divisional and district level, and access PoPs at upazila or neighbourhood level. The licence rollout obligation is measured by upazila coverage.

t: What does a PoP network map show?
b: PoP locations, the fibre routes and rings linking them, and the capacity or technology at each site.

t: Who uses a PoP network map, and for what?
b: Sales teams use it to check whether a client site is serviceable. Planners use it to find coverage gaps and single-homed sites. Operations use it to trace the impact of a fibre cut.

t: What decides where a new PoP is placed?
b: Client demand (mobile towers, ISPs, banks, government offices), distance limits such as about 20 km for GPON, existing fibre routes and rings, right of way, reliable power, and rollout obligations.

t: How do PoPs appear in the MPLS lab topology?
b: Each named router sits at a site: Badda-PE and Badda-P at the Badda PoP in Dhaka, with MGRE-P and the remote NTTN-PE reaching out towards the edge. The loopback /32 address is what identifies each PoP router in the network.

t: What is the backbone?
b: The high-capacity network linking PoPs across cities and districts. It carries the aggregated traffic of many clients over DWDM and IP/MPLS.

t: What is the last mile?
b: The final link from the nearest PoP to the individual client site or end user, usually GPON, point-to-point fibre or wireless.

t: What is the middle mile?
b: The aggregation segment between the two: metro and district rings that collect traffic from access PoPs and carry it to the core.

t: How do backbone and last mile differ in capacity, technology, cost and failure impact?
b: Aspect Backbone Last mile Capacity 10G to 100G+ per link, shared Mbps to a few Gbps per client Technology DWDM, OTN, IP/MPLS GPON, point-to-point fibre, wireless Topology Rings and mesh Tree or single drop Cost driver Long routes, high-end equipment Number of drops, civil work per client Failure impact Many clients and districts One client or building

t: In the MPLS decks, which elements are backbone and which are last mile?
b: The PE and P routers with their OSPF, LDP and BGP sessions form the backbone. The attachment circuit, the PE interface to the CE such as TE0/0/10, G0/0/15 or vlan69, is the last-mile hand-off.

t: Who provides last mile and backbone in Bangladesh's layered model?
b: NTTN operators provide backbone and fibre transmission. ISPs and mobile operators own the retail relationship with end users, and lease fibre from NTTN operators rather than laying their own.

t: Why is the last mile often the weakest and costliest part per user?
b: It has the most individual links, usually with no alternate path, built through dense streets and buildings. Each drop serves few users, so cost and fault exposure per user are highest there.

t: What is the difference between redundancy and resilience?
b: Redundancy is having spare components or paths. Resilience is the network's ability to keep delivering service through a failure and recover quickly, which redundancy makes possible.

t: What is path diversity, and why must the two paths be physically separate?
b: Two routes between the same points along different roads or ducts. If both fibres share one trench or pole line, a single cut takes down both, so logical redundancy without physical diversity gives no protection.

t: What is the difference between protection and restoration?
b: Protection uses a pre-provisioned backup and switches in about 50 ms. Restoration computes a new path after the failure, which is slower but uses spare capacity more efficiently.

t: What do 1+1 and 1:1 protection mean?
b: In 1+1 the signal is sent on both paths at once and the receiver picks the better one. In 1:1 the backup path is reserved but idle, or carrying low-priority traffic, until the working path fails.

t: Which mechanisms provide resilience at each layer?
b: Optical: 1+1 optical protection and ROADM restoration. SDH: SNCP and MS-SPRing. IP/MPLS: OSPF reconvergence, Fast Reroute or LFA, and LDP-IGP sync. Service: dual-homing a client to two PEs, and redundant route reflectors.

t: Which resilience features appear in the lab configurations?
b: fast-reroute lfa under OSPF on the P router, mpls ldp sync so traffic uses a link only when labels are ready, loopback-sourced BGP sessions that survive a single link failure, and tuned OSPF costs (1, 10, 500) that make the tunnel a higher-cost path.

t: What is a single point of failure in the lab topology?
b: Badda-P is the only route reflector and the only path between Badda-PE and MGRE-P, and the four routers form a chain, not a ring. A production network would add a second RR and an alternate path.

t: How is availability measured, and what does 99.99% mean?
b: As the percentage of time a service is up, driven by how often failures occur (MTBF) and how fast they are repaired (MTTR). 99.99% allows about 53 minutes of downtime per year.

t: Why does underground versus overhead fibre matter for resilience in Bangladesh?
b: Overhead cable is far more exposed to cuts, storms, fire and road work. The BTRC chairman has criticised NTTN licensees' use of overhead fibre as a service-quality concern. A figure of only 15% to 17% of the two private NTTNs' fibre being underground was attributed to him in the original set; it was not confirmed in the sources opened, so treat it as unverified.

t: End of Service Benefit Policy: purpose and entitlement
b:
End of Service (EOS) Benefit is a long-term financial benefit paid to a permanent employee on separation, together with the final settlement, in recognition of long-term contribution to the company. Policy name: "Fiber@Home Employees' End of Service Benefit". Version 01, owner HR Department, dated 2 January 2024, effective 1 January 2024. It replaces the 'Gratuity' policy circulated on 9 July 2023, which was cancelled (the Board approved EOS in lieu of Gratuity in November 2023).
Entitlement (clause 2):
a. A permanent employee with at least 5 (five) years of continuous service as a permanent employee (as on 1 January 2024, or who completes the 5 years later) is eligible.
b. If an employee rejoins, service for EOS is counted from the date of rejoining.
c. A permanent employee who dies before completing 5 years is eligible for EOS equal to the completed years of service.
d. Satisfactory performance in every evaluation year is required for the full benefit. Each employee gets a satisfactory-performance certificate signed by the Line Manager and Next Line Manager (HOF/HOD). A year rated unsatisfactory under the policy does not count for EOS.
e. An employee who receives 2 (two) warning letters, or any other disciplinary punishment (increment hold, downgradation, fine etc.) approved by the Managing Director, in a year loses EOS for that year. Example in the policy: an employee completing 5 years who falls under 2(e) in one year is paid last drawn basic salary x 1.0 x 4 (that is, 5 minus 1 years).
f. An employee discontinued from service immediately gets no EOS for that year.
g. An employee dismissed from the company, or convicted of a criminal offence by a penal court, is not eligible.
h. An employee who commits suicide is not eligible.
src: HR Policy: End of Service Benefit Policy (v01, effective 1 Jan 2024; amended 4 Sep 2024)

t: End of Service Benefit: payment scale and calculation
b:
Clause 3 (Payment). EOS = total completed years of service from the date of joining (no fraction of a year is counted) x last drawn basic salary x a multiplier set by length of service:
- 05 years and above, up to 10 years: last drawn basic salary x 1.0 x length of service in years.
- 10 years and above, up to 15 years: last drawn basic salary x 1.25 x length of service in years.
- 15 years and above: last drawn basic salary x 1.5 x length of service in years.
Note: the scale is written with overlapping boundaries (10 and 15 years appear in two bands); the policy text does not say which band applies at exactly 10 or 15 years. Ask HR.
Amendment (Ref F@H/NOA/HR/2024-25/04, dated 4 September 2024, effective 1 July 2024): clause 3 was changed to align with the Bangladesh Labour Act 2006. The original wording said the benefit was paid "including grossing up withholding tax". The amended wording removes the gross-up: any applicable income tax on this benefit is payable by the employee and is adjusted with the final payment.
Effective date (clause 4): the policy applies from 1 January 2024; management may amend it when business requires.
src: HR Policy: End of Service Benefit Policy (v01, effective 1 Jan 2024; amended 4 Sep 2024)
